content: Errors in the placement of EKG leads can lead to significant misinterpretations of the electrocardiogram (ECG) and potentially incorrect clinical conclusions. Below are detailed descriptions of common lead placement errors and their effects on the ECG: 1. Right and Left Arm Lead Reversal: When the right arm and left arm leads are switched, the ECG will show negative QRS complexes in lead I. This can mimic a right axis deviation, which may lead to an incorrect diagnosis. This type of error is one of the most frequently encountered mistakes in clinical practice. 2. Right Leg and Right Arm Lead Reversal: If the right leg and right arm leads are reversed, lead II will show minimal or no signal. 3. Reversal of Leads II and III: This can lead to confusion in interpreting the inferior leads. 4. Reversal of Leads aVR and aVL: When leads aVR and aVL are reversed, the augmented limb leads will display incorrect polarity, leading to misinterpretation of the lateral and right-sided electrical activity. 5. Left Arm and Left Leg Lead Reversal: Reversing the left arm and left leg leads will cause: Reversal of leads I and II. Reversal of leads aVR and aVF. Inversion of lead III. These changes can mimic pathological conditions, such as axis deviations or conduction abnormalities. 6. Right Arm and Left Leg Lead Reversal: If the right arm and left leg leads are switched, the following changes will occur: Inversion of leads I, II, and III. Reversal of leads aVR and aVF. These alterations can significantly distort the ECG and lead to misdiagnosis. 7. Distinguishing Lead Reversal from Dextrocardia: Dextrocardia, a rare congenital condition where the heart is positioned on the right side of the chest, can sometimes mimic lead reversal. The key to differentiation lies in the precordial leads: In dextrocardia, there will be an R wave inversion across the precordial leads (V1–V6). In lead reversal, the precordial R wave progression remains normal. Examples of Lead Reversal: Right and Left Arm Lead Reversal: This can be differentiated from dextrocardia by examining the precordial R wave progression. In lead reversal, the precordial leads will not show the characteristic R wave inversion seen in dextrocardia. Right Arm and Left Leg Lead Reversal: This results in an abnormal ECG tracing. References and Resources: Hammill SC, Electrocardiographic Diagnoses: Criteria and Definitions of Abnormalities, Chapter 18, Mayo Clinic Concise Textbook of Cardiology, 3rd edition, 2007. ISBN: 0-8493-9057-5. Additional resources include ECGpedia, the 12-lead ECG library, and simulation tools for studying the relationship between cardiac electrical activity and the ECG.
